translations.text: There are many countless kinds of creatures throughout the world, whose natures we cannot rightly recount, nor can we know their number.

So widely throughout the world are the far-spread multitudes of birds and earth-treading beasts, as far as the water, the roaring sea and the surge of salt waves, encircles this bright bosom of the earth.
We have heard tell of the wondrous nature of one wild creature, renowned among men, which dwells in its home in distant lands and enjoys its native land among the mountain caves.
That beast is called the panther by name, as the children of men, men firm in wisdom, make known in writings about that lone wanderer.
He is a friend to everyone and generous with good gifts, except to the dragon alone. He is always hostile to the dragon and lives by every harm he can do to it.
That is a wondrous beast, wonderfully beautiful in every hue. Just as men say, holy men, that Joseph's tunic was of every dye, shifting in colours,
Each of those bright colours shone more distinct than the next to the children of men. In the same way the beast's coat, bright in every shade, shines wonderfully brighter and fairer,
so that each colour is more wonderful than the next, more distinct still and fairer, and gleams with adornments, ever more marvellous. He has a special nature: gentle and moderate.
He is meek, lovable and kindly, and he will do no harm to anyone except the poisonous enemy, his ancient adversary, of whom I spoke before.

He is always glad to eat his fill. When he has taken food, after the meal he looks for rest in a hidden place under the mountain caves. There the warrior of the people sleeps for the space of three nights, overcome by slumber.
Then, bold in courage and full of glory, he quickly rises up from sleep on the third day. A melodious sound, the most delightful of voices, comes out of the wild beast's mouth.

after that voice a fragrance comes out of that place, a delightful vapour, sweeter and stronger than every scent, than the blossoms of plants and the blooms of the woods, nobler than all the adornments of the earth.

Then from cities and royal seats and from castle halls many a troop of men travel along the roads of the earth in throngs of peoples and in bands of horsemen, hurrying in haste, spear-warriors. In the same way the animals follow that voice toward the fragrance.
So is the Lord God, ruler of joys, gentle to all other creatures, to every one of the hosts, except the dragon alone, the source of venom.
That is the ancient enemy, whom he bound in the abyss of torments and fettered with fiery chains, covered with dire constraints; and on the third day he rose from the hidden place,
after he had suffered death for us for three nights, the prince of angels, the giver of victories. That was a sweet fragrance, beautiful and delightful throughout all the world.
Afterwards righteous men thronged in crowds to that fragrance from every side, throughout the whole circuit of the earth's regions.

As the wise Saint Paul said: "Manifold and abundant throughout the world are the good things which the Father almighty, the only hope of all creatures above and below, deals out to us as a gift and as sustenance for life." That is a noble fragrance.
